prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN)  -- British Airways is asking thousands of its staff to work for free for up to four weeks, spokeswoman Kirsten Millard said Tuesday. British Airways plans to reduce capacity by 4 percent next winter by parking up to 16 aircraft. In an e-mail to all its staff, the airline offered workers between one and four weeks of unpaid leave -- but with the option to work during this period. British Airways employs just more than 40,000 people in the United Kingdom. Last month, the company posted a record annual loss of £400 million ($656 million). Its chief executive declared at the time there were "absolutely no signs of recovery" in the industry. "In 30 years in this business and I've never seen anything like this. This is by far the biggest crisis the industry has ever faced," said Willie Walsh, British Airways' chief executive.  Watch more about BA's request » . A spokesman for one of Britain's biggest unions said its workers could not afford to work for free for a month. "It's all well and good for Willie Walsh to say he's prepared to work for free when he earns four times in a month what they do in a year," said Ciaran Naidoo, a spokesman for Unite. He pointed out that the airline was not ordering staff to work without pay. "It's a request -- you can take unpaid leave or you can work for free, and the chances of people working for free are very unlikely, but there might be some people who want to take unpaid leave." Demand for the airline's passenger seats and cargo holds fell during the last financial year, while its fuel bill rocketed to almost £3 billion ($4.7 billion). Walsh said British Airways' woes were inextricably linked to the downturn in the global economy and that there had been no sign of any "green shoots" of recovery. Like its premium-class competitors, British Airways is losing customers to cheaper rivals. The airline's premium passenger numbers fell 13 percent in the second half of last year, in line with the industry average. Total traffic fell 3.4 percent and while the airline carried 33.1 million passengers last year, it was a drop of 4.3 percent from the previous year. The dip in demand for British Airways' flights has forced a switch in strategy at the airline. From the end of last year, it has been trying to tempt passengers with lower fares, sacrificing profit per seat for "bums on seats." It plans to reduce capacity by 4 percent next winter by parking up to 16 aircraft. CNN's Alysen Miller contributed to this report.

“It’s a request — you can take unpaid leave or you can work for free, and the chances of people working for free are very unlikely, but there might be some people who want to take unpaid leave,” he said.

Demand for the airline’s passenger seats and cargo capacity fell during the last financial year, while its fuel bill soared to almost £3 billion ($4.7 billion).

Walsh said British Airways’ difficulties were closely tied to the downturn in the global economy and that there had been no sign of any “green shoots” of recovery.

The drop in demand for British Airways flights has prompted a shift in the airline’s strategy. Since the end of last year, it has been trying to attract passengers with lower fares, sacrificing profit per seat in favor of filling more seats.

**LONDON — British Airways Cuts Winter Capacity, Parks Aircraft and Asks Staff to Work Without Pay Amid Industry Downturn**

**LONDON, June 17** — British Airways is moving to deepen cost-cutting measures as the global airline industry faces one of its sharpest downturns in decades, with the carrier reducing winter flight capacity, grounding aircraft and asking thousands of employees to consider working without pay.

The airline, one of Europe’s largest long-haul carriers, has been hit hard by a steep fall in passenger demand, weaker premium travel and volatile fuel costs. Business-class and first-class bookings — traditionally a crucial source of profit for British Airways — have dropped sharply as companies cut travel budgets during the economic slowdown.

As part of its response, British Airways plans to reduce capacity during the winter season, including trimming flight frequencies on some routes and parking aircraft that would otherwise remain in service. The measures are intended to bring the airline’s flying schedule closer into line with reduced demand and to limit operating losses during the traditionally weaker winter months.

Company executives have warned that the downturn is severe and that the airline must act quickly to preserve cash. British Airways has already reported heavy losses and has been working to lower costs across its network, from fuel use and aircraft deployment to staffing and administrative expenses.

In a highly unusual step, the company has also asked employees to volunteer for unpaid work or unpaid leave. Staff have been invited to take options including unpaid leave, reduced working hours or, in some cases, working for a period without salary. The airline has framed the request as a voluntary measure designed to help protect jobs and reduce the need for compulsory redundancies.

The request has drawn widespread attention because of its stark nature: asking employees to help the airline financially by giving up pay during a period of intense pressure. British Airways has said senior executives are also participating in pay-related sacrifices, including unpaid work or salary reductions, as part of the broader effort to cut costs.

Union representatives and employee groups have reacted cautiously, noting that many airline workers are already under financial strain. While some staff may accept unpaid leave or temporary reductions in hours, unions have traditionally opposed measures that shift the burden of corporate losses onto employees. They have also raised concerns about whether voluntary schemes could become a precursor to deeper job cuts if trading conditions do not improve.

The airline industry as a whole has been battered by the global recession. Passenger numbers have fallen, cargo volumes have weakened and airlines have struggled to fill seats at profitable fares. Carriers across Europe, North America and Asia have announced capacity cuts, aircraft groundings, hiring freezes and job reductions. Many airlines have also deferred aircraft deliveries or sought new financing to strengthen their balance sheets.

British Airways is particularly exposed to the downturn in premium travel because of its reliance on transatlantic business routes and high-yield corporate customers. The London–New York market, long one of the most lucrative corridors in global aviation, has seen demand fall as banks, law firms and multinational companies reduce travel spending.

Parking aircraft is one of the most visible signs of the slowdown. By grounding planes, airlines can reduce variable costs such as fuel, maintenance and crew expenses, though parked aircraft still generate financing, leasing and storage costs. Capacity reductions also allow carriers to avoid flying half-empty aircraft, which can quickly deepen losses.

The planned winter cuts are expected to affect selected routes and frequencies rather than amount to a complete withdrawal from major markets. British Airways is likely to focus reductions where demand has weakened most or where flights are less profitable. The carrier must also balance cuts against the need to preserve valuable airport slots, particularly at London Heathrow, where takeoff and landing rights are scarce and strategically important.

For passengers, the immediate effects may include fewer flight options on some routes, schedule changes and the use of smaller aircraft in certain markets. However, airlines typically try to protect core business routes and long-haul services where demand remains comparatively resilient.

The cost-cutting drive comes as British Airways seeks to position itself for a recovery while surviving the downturn. The company has been pursuing broader strategic measures, including closer cooperation with partner airlines and efforts to improve efficiency. But management has made clear that near-term survival depends heavily on reducing costs and matching capacity to demand.

Industry analysts say the airline’s actions reflect the scale of the crisis confronting full-service carriers. Unlike low-cost airlines, which rely more heavily on short-haul leisure traffic and leaner operating models, legacy carriers such as British Airways carry higher fixed costs and are more vulnerable to collapses in premium revenue.

The decision to ask employees to work without pay may help British Airways conserve cash, but it also risks damaging morale at a time when staff cooperation is essential. Cabin crew, pilots, engineers, ground staff and administrative employees all play critical roles in maintaining operations, and prolonged uncertainty could intensify labor tensions.

Still, British Airways executives have argued that extraordinary measures are necessary. With demand weak and no clear timeline for a full recovery, the airline is seeking to avoid more drastic restructuring by securing short-term savings wherever possible.

The coming winter will be a key test. If passenger demand stabilizes, the capacity reductions and voluntary staff concessions may help the airline weather the downturn. But if travel continues to weaken, British Airways — like many of its global rivals — may face pressure to take even deeper action, including further aircraft groundings, route cuts and job losses.

## British Airways’ Recession-Era Troubles: Industry Report

British Airways entered the global financial crisis in a weakened position, hit by a sharp fall in passenger demand, high fuel costs, and pressure to reduce capacity and labour expenses. The downturn exposed the airline’s dependence on premium business travel and forced management to seek major cost savings from staff and operations.

### Financial pressure and falling demand

During the recession, British Airways suffered one of the worst financial periods in its history. For the year to March 2009, the airline reported a pre-tax loss of about **£401 million**, compared with a profit the previous year. The result reflected a severe deterioration in trading conditions, particularly in long-haul and premium markets.

Passenger numbers declined as both businesses and leisure travellers cut spending. The most damaging fall was in **premium traffic**, including first- and business-class passengers, which traditionally generated a large share of BA’s profits. In 2009, BA regularly reported double-digit declines in premium passenger volumes, with some monthly figures showing premium traffic down by more than 15% year on year.

Overall passenger traffic also weakened. The airline carried fewer passengers as the recession reduced demand across key routes, especially transatlantic services, which were central to BA’s earnings.

### Fuel costs added to the strain

Although oil prices fell from their 2008 peaks during the recession, British Airways still faced a very large fuel bill because of earlier high prices and hedging positions. For the 2008–09 financial year, BA’s fuel costs rose sharply, reaching close to **£3 billion**, an increase of hundreds of millions of pounds from the previous year.

The combination of weaker revenues and elevated fuel costs created a severe squeeze on margins. Fuel remained one of the airline’s largest operating expenses and limited its ability to respond flexibly to falling demand.

### Staff pay and cost-cutting proposals

In response, BA management sought major labour cost reductions. The airline introduced or proposed measures including:

- **A pay freeze** for thousands of employees  
- **Voluntary unpaid leave**  
- **Voluntary part-time working**  
- **Voluntary redundancy programmes**  
- Requests for staff to consider working without pay for a period or taking unpaid leave  

Chief executive Willie Walsh publicly framed the measures as necessary to protect the airline’s finances and preserve jobs during an unprecedented downturn. He also said he would work without pay for a month, a symbolic gesture intended to demonstrate management’s commitment to cost reduction.

BA asked employees across the company to contribute to savings, arguing that lower labour costs were essential if the airline was to survive the crisis in a competitive position.

### Union reaction

The proposals triggered strong opposition from unions, particularly **Unite**, which represented many cabin crew and ground staff. Union leaders criticised the idea of employees working without pay, arguing that staff should not be expected to absorb the consequences of the crisis while the company pursued restructuring.

Unite described some of the proposals as unreasonable and warned that compulsory changes to pay, staffing levels, or working conditions could provoke industrial action. The union accepted that the airline faced difficult market conditions but argued that cost-saving measures should be negotiated rather than imposed.

Tensions between BA and its workforce intensified over the period, contributing to wider labour disputes that later affected the airline’s operations and reputation.

### Capacity reductions and operational response

British Airways also reduced capacity to match weaker demand. The airline cut flight frequencies, reduced available seats, and grounded aircraft on underperforming routes. Capacity reductions were focused particularly on winter schedules and long-haul markets where premium demand had fallen sharply.

BA announced cuts amounting to several percentage points of total capacity, including reductions in both short-haul and long-haul flying. The aim was to improve load factors, reduce operating costs, and limit losses from flying half-empty aircraft.

The airline also continued efforts to simplify its network, defer spending where possible, and concentrate on routes with stronger revenue potential.

### Industry significance

BA’s recession-era problems reflected broader pressures across the airline industry, but the carrier was especially exposed because of its reliance on premium long-haul passengers. The collapse in business travel, combined with high fuel costs and rigid labour expenses, forced the airline into aggressive cost-cutting.

The episode highlighted several industry lessons:

- Premium traffic can fall faster than overall passenger demand in a recession.  
- Fuel-price volatility can damage airline finances even when demand is already weak.  
- Labour relations become critical when airlines seek rapid cost reductions.  
- Capacity discipline is essential during downturns to protect yields and cash flow.  

British Airways’ response—pay restraint, unpaid leave proposals, job reductions, and capacity cuts—was part of a broader attempt to stabilise the company during one of the most difficult periods in modern aviation.
